title: Short-term exposure to sublethal tebuconazole induces physiological impairment in male zebrafish (Danio rerio).
text_summary: 本文评估亚致死浓度戊唑醇对雄性斑马鱼生理状态的短期影响及转入清水后的恢复。鱼暴露于230 μg/L戊唑醇7或14天，再恢复相同时间。暴露提高卵黄蛋白原、葡萄糖、乳酸、胆固醇和甘油三酯，并改变多种肝脏和代谢相关酶活性；部分指标在14天恢复后正常化，但甘油三酯、乳酸和部分酶活性仍异常，卵黄蛋白原甚至继续升高。结果说明戊唑醇可同时干扰内分泌和中间代谢，现有恢复期不足以完全恢复鱼类生理。

Short-term exposure to sublethal tebuconazole induces physiological
impairment in male zebraﬁsh (Danio rerio)
E. Sancho , M.J. Villarroel, C. Fernández, E. Andreu, M.D. Ferrando
Laboratory for Ecotoxicology, Department of Functional Biology, Faculty of Biological Sciences, University of Valencia, Dr. Moliner-50, E46100-Burjassot (Valencia), Spain

a r t i c l e in f o

a b s t r a c t

Article history:
Received 25 November 2008
Received in revised form
24 September 2009
Accepted 26 September 2009
Available online 7 November 2009

The aim of the present study was to assess the physiological response of male zebraﬁsh Danio rerio to
the fungicide tebuconazole and recovery in fungicide-free water. Acute toxicity tests were carried out
and the median lethal concentration (LC50) from 24 to 96 h was calculated. The ﬁsh were exposed to a
sublethal fungicide concentration of 230 mg/L for 7 or 14 days and allowed to recover for 7 or 14 more
days, respectively. Whole-body levels of vitellogenins, triglycerides, cholesterol, glucose, lactate and
proteins as well as the activities g-glutamil transpeptidase (g-GT), alanin aminotransferase (AlAT),
alkaline phosphatase (AP) and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) were assayed; corpulence factor (k) was
also calculated. Fish exhibited signiﬁcant increase of vitellogenins (Vtg), which continued to increase
after 14 days of recovery. Levels of glucose, lactate, cholesterol and triglycerides increased after 7 and 14
days of exposure. Finally, cholesterol and glucose recovered after 14 days of recovery whereas
triglycerides and lactate continued to be elevated. Proteins and k remained unaltered the entire
experiments. AAT, AlAT and AP enhanced during exposure and did not recover at the end (except AlAT).
A longer recovery period should be necessary to re-establish ﬁsh physiology. These results alert about
the multiple disruptive physiological actions that tebuconazole may have on ﬁsh.

Keywords:
Endocrine disruption
Fungicide
Intermediary metabolism
Tebuconazole
Vitellogenin
Zebraﬁsh

1. Introduction
Current-used pesticides (CUPs) can be deﬁned as those modern
pesticides that are currently registered for use, generally developed from chemical synthesis, and typically used in the
agriculture or lawn care sector (Konwick et al., 2006). Tebuconazole is widely used as fungicide in paddy ﬁelds from Eastern Spain
among the Spanish Mediterranean wetlands to avoid and treat
rice blast disease caused by Pyricularia oryzae. Tebuconazole
(commercial name Folicurs) is classiﬁed as toxic to aquatic
organisms that may cause long-term adverse effects in the aquatic
environment (Bayer CropScience Limited, 2005). It is widely used
as an alternative to tricyclazole and prochloraz treatments in
paddy ﬁelds from Eastern Spain among the Spanish Mediterranean wetlands to avoid and treat rice blast disease during July and
early August. Information about the environmental fate of
tebuconazole is scarce. Konwick et al. (2006) estimated a halflife of one day for tebuconazole in rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus
mykiss) under laboratory conditions joint to a time to 95% of
elimination (t95) for this fungicide of 4.5 days. However, half-lives
of 24 and 22 days have been determined in zebraﬁsh (Danio rerio)
and water, respectively (Andreu et al., under review). During the

spraying operations with the commercial Folicurs (25EW)
residual concentrations of tebuconazole, while not acutely toxic,
had been detected for more than 5 days after the end of
treatments (Andreu et al., under review).
The literature indicates that triazole fungicides as well as
related imidazoles are used for protection of cereals. Their
fungicidal effect is a result of inhibition of cytochrome P450
(CYP450) dependent C14 demethylation of lanosterol, an intermediate in ergosterol biosynthesis and interfering with the
synthesis of sterols, which are essential for the construction of
normal cell membranes. In ﬁsh, CYP-mediated steroid metabolism, in addition to xenobiotic metabolism, can be altered
(Konwick et al., 2006).
Fish are particularly sensitive to the inﬂuence of pesticides
because they are able to uptake and retain dissolved xenobiotic in
water via active or passive processes. The physiological changes
associated with ﬁsh response to environmental low pesticide
levels not only provide a mean to understand environmental
levels of pollutants in biological terms, but also can be used as
model for vertebrate toxicity including man.
The dynamics of intermediary metabolism are greatly inﬂuenced by any sort of stressors (any sort of change altering the
homeostasis of the animal), which can lead to a group of
responses referred to as stress response (Heath, 1995). The stress
responses are adaptative and usually help animals to cope with
changes in their environment. However, sometimes, modiﬁcations


ARTICLE IN PRESS
E. Sancho et al. / Ecotoxicology and Environmental Safety 73 (2010) 370–376

of stress response or harmful effects derived of it can have serious
consequences at the individual level and ﬁnally at the population
level.
Chemicals that mimic endocrine functional molecules have
caused great concern because of their effects on endocrine
systems in man and wildlife. Prochloraz, an imidazole fungicide,
proved to possess anti-estrogenic effect on D. rerio (Kinnberg
et al., 2007). In mammals a similar pattern of toxicity for
prochloraz and tebuconazole as pro-feminization effects has been
demonstrated (Taxvig et al., 2007). Recently, tricyclazole has
proved its endocrine reproduction effect among other disruptive
effects on ﬁsh physiology in zebraﬁsh (D. rerio) as investigated
in our laboratory (Sancho et al, 2009a). Therefore, it appears
promising to study the effect of this relevant triazole in ﬁsh
physiology during a short-term exposure in order to elucidate
harmful effects on health of the individuals and possible
consequences.
Zebraﬁsh (D. rerio) was selected as test organisms in this study
because it is considered as one alternative species for the
evaluation of anthropogenic chemicals and widespread use in
biological studies. It has been also proposed as a test organism by
the OECD (1998).
The purpose of the present research was to study the impact of
a short and continuous exposure of a sublethal concentration of
tebuconazole for D. rerio. Investigated were key biomarkers
involved in different physiological pathways as biomarkers of
fungicide poisoning and their recovery after 7 or 14 days of
exposure of the ﬁsh in fungicide-free water. Some biomarkers of
intermediary metabolism and detoxiﬁcation induction, joint to
reproductive disruption were used as key indicators of fungicide
exposure.

2. Material and methods
2.1. Ethical statement
The University of Valencia (Spain) guaranties that all the experimental ﬁsh
used in the present study were maintained in the laboratory following national
and institutional guidelines for the protection of animal welfare in accordance
with our Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.

2.2. Test animals
Zebraﬁsh (D. rerio) stocks were purchased from a commercial ﬁsh supplier
(Fauna Acuatica, Valencia, Spain). Fish were acclimatized for two weeks to
laboratory conditions in 300-L glass tanks before the start of the experiments
following the guideline of OECD (1998). During the acclimatization period, the ﬁsh
were fed twice a day with a semi-synthetic diet of ﬁsh food (Tetramin). Adult male
ﬁsh (Mean 7SEM length and weight 3.20 70.28 cm and 0.507 0.09 g, respectively) were used for this study. All the animals were healthy; a mortality of less
than 3% was observed in the stocks used during the acclimatization period.

2.3. Dilution water
The tanks were supplied with a continuous ﬂow of dechlorinated tap water
(total hardness: 2407 10 mg/L as CaCO3 according to the Merck classiﬁcation,
Aquamerck 8039, Germany; pH 7.97 0.2 using a Crison pHmeter; alkalinity
4.07 0.5 mmol/L, Aquamerck 11109, Germany). The temperature was 25 7 1 1C and
the light regime was 12 h light:12 h dark (Roex et al., 2003).

2.4. Test chemical
Stock solutions were prepared by dissolving technical grade tebuconazole
(chemical name IUPAC: (RS)-1-p-chlorophenyl)-4,4-dimethyl-3-3(1H-1,2,4-triazol1-ylmethyl) pentan-3-ol) with a purity of 96% in acetone (Pesticide Residue
Analysis Grade). Pesticide was obtained from Bayer CropScience Limited. Solid
phase extraction-gas chromatography analysis (SPE-GC/MSMS) conﬁrmed the
presence of tebuconazole in the water (90%) over the entire exposure time. Water

371

analysis determined that the tebuconazole-measured concentrations were very
close to nominal concentrations (217.0 7 7.6 mg/L, Andreu et al., under review).
2.5. Toxicity testing protocol
Four-day static acute toxicity tests were performed in our laboratory to
determine the LC50 values of tebuconazole in D. rerio (OECD guidelines, 1998).
Fungicide concentrations of 15, 18, 20, 23 and 25 mg/L were used. After
being acclimatized to laboratory conditions adult male ﬁsh were randomly
distributed in each test aquarium. For each concentration, a group of 10 randomly
selected ﬁsh was placed in the glass tanks (10 L per tank of continuous
aerated water). This procedure was repeated three times for each concentration.
The control zebraﬁsh groups were kept in clean water as in the experimental
sets. During the acute toxicity test (96 h) animals were not fed. The number of
dead ﬁsh was recorded at 24, 48, 72 and 96 h. Dead ﬁsh were removed from the
tanks.
2.6. Sub-acute short-term test
A sub-lethal test concentration of 1/100 LC50-24 h (230 mg/L) was used for the
assessment of tebuconazole physiological and biochemical effects on ﬁsh. The
experiments were carried out in a continuous ﬂow-through system, based on
OECD guidelines (1998). For the exposure period, tebuconazole was dissolved in
acetone and the solution was supplied to a glass mixing chamber with tap water
and connected to a perfusor pump (Gilson, Minipulse 3) that generated a constant
solution ﬂow. The outlet was connected to a 100-L glass test aquarium, diluting the
pesticide to the desired concentration (230 mg/L) by a constant water ﬂow. Flow
rates were checked once daily, and there were approximately three volume
changes per 24 h (Sancho et al., 2009a). This system was connected 48 h before the
start of the experiments to reach a balance of tebuconazole contaminated water in
the test aquaria. Final concentration of solvent (acetone) in the test aquarium was
o17 mL/L.
Previous studies carried out in our laboratory (unpublished data) indicated
that the amount of acetone (17 mL/L) used as solvent during 14 days did not disturb
either enzyme activity or biochemical–physiological parameters measured in
zebraﬁsh.
Fish were fed twice a day during the entire experiments with commercial ﬁsh
food (Tetramin) at a level of approximately 1% of their body weight per day (Roex
et al., 2003). Based on the conditions published in Sancho et al. (2009a), two
different experiments were carried out as follows:
Experiment 1: Zebraﬁsh individuals (total number= 12) were exposed in 2
different tanks (100 L) for one week to 230 mg/L of fungicide. After 7 days of
exposure, six zebraﬁsh were randomly removed, rinsed with tap water, euthanized
with MS-222 (Kinnberg et al., 2007), weighed, measured and stored frozen
( 80 1C). In a second part of the experiment, the other six zebraﬁsh pre-exposed
for 7 days to tebuconazole were transferred to clean water in a 100 L glass aquaria
with the same ﬂow-through system under the above-described conditions but
without fungicide (recovery period). Fish were removed after 7 days in these
conditions, total length (l) and total weigh (w) pointed out and stored frozen
( 80 1C) until analysis. Control groups with the same amount of acetone were
kept in 100 L test aquaria in the same experimental conditions but without
fungicide.
Experiment 2: Zebraﬁsh individuals (total number = 18) in 3 different tanks
(100 L) were exposed for two weeks to 230 mg/L of tebuconazole. After 14 days
of fungicide exposure, six zebraﬁsh were removed, rinsed with tap water,
euthanized with MS222 (Kinnberg et al., 2007), weighed and measured. At the
14th day, an exposed group of ﬁsh was transferred to a different aquaria with
clean water for a recovery period in the same conditions described for experiment 1. At the 7th and the 14th day of that recovery period, six extra zebraﬁsh
were removed, rinsed with dilution water, euthanized, weighed, measured and
stored frozen ( 80 1C) until further analysis. A control group with the same
amount of acetone was kept in 100 L test aquaria in the same experimental
conditions but without fungicide and they were sampled at the same experimental
times.
2.7. Analysis procedures
2.7.1. Tebuconazole determination
Tebuconazole concentration in the experimental water was determined in the
Agrarian Laboratory of the Generalitat Valenciana (Spain) by Gas-chromatography/
MassSpectrophotometry techniques (GC–MS/MS) as in Andreu et al., under
review.
Water samples were collected from the tank and stored in amber glass bottles
(250 mL). GF/F Whatman glass microﬁber ﬁlters were used to eliminate organic
matter and ﬁsh detritus in the water samples. The samples were kept frozen until
the analysis. In order to extract the residues of tebuconazole from water samples,
extraction cartridges (500 mg of C18-phase) were used. The solid phase was
conditioned with three portions of methanol (3 mL) and three portions of


ARTICLE IN PRESS
E. Sancho et al. / Ecotoxicology and Environmental Safety 73 (2010) 370–376

water (3 mL). Between 10 and 50 mL of the sample were passed through C18phase with a ﬂow of 1 mL/min. The solid phase was dried (15 min, dry nitrogen
stream), and the tebuconazole extracted with three portions of 1 mL acetone.
Finally, the tebuconazole solution was poured in a gas chromatography vial and
kept.
Residues of tebuconazole in the water were measured using a gas
chromatograph 6890N (Agilent technologies, USA) equipped with a mass-selective
detector 5975 (Agilent Technologies) and autosampler 7683 Series (Agilent
Technologies, USA). Separations were carried out on capillary column HP-5MS
(30 m  0.25 mm  0.25 mm, Agilent Technologies, USA). All GC–MS chromatographic data were processed using ChemStation Software (Hewlett-Packard, USA)
equipped with a NIST 2005 Mass spectral library. Helium (purity 99.9999%)
was used as carrier and collision gas; the injector and detector operating
temperatures were 280 and 180 1C, respectively. The column oven temperature
was 280 1C. The detection time was 11.1 min. MS detector was equipped with a
quadrupole analyzer operating in electron ionization mode (EI); ion source
temperature was 230 1C and MS Quad temperature was 150 1C. In these conditions
tebuconazole recoveries from water were not less than 90% (Andreu et al., under
review).
Pesticide-grade solvents (acetone, acetonitrile, methanol, dichlormethane,
n-hexane) and pesticide anhydrous sodium sulphate were provide by Scharlau,
S.A. (Barcelona, Spain). The water used for the extraction of pesticide was
Milli-Q-Plus puriﬁed. C18 (solid phase extraction-—SPE) cartridges were provided
by J.T. Baker (Barcelona, Spain).
2.7.2. Biochemical determinations
All biochemical determinations were performed according to automated
spectrophotometric Kit methods provided by Spinreact, S.A. (Spain) using a
Chemistry Proﬁle Analyzer (C.P.A.; Coulter Scientiﬁc, Margency, France). Spintrol
Calibrator (ref. 1002010) and Spintrol ‘‘H’’ Normal (ref. 1002120) were used for the
calibration of the apparatus and as serum components control, respectively.
Each individual ﬁsh was homogenized with ﬁve volumes of 0.1 M phosphate
buffer (pH 7.2 at 0 1C). The homogenates were centrifuged at 1666g (4 1C) for
10 min and the resulting supernatants were diluted ﬁve-fold with phosphate
buffer and assayed rapidly for determinations.
The following parameters were determined after each experiment:
 Metabolites of the intermediary metabolism: Glucose, lactate, cholesterol, total
proteins and triglycerides were selected as intermediate metabolic substrates.
The Spinreact cholesterol CHOD-POD Kit (ref. 1001093) was used to determine
cholesterol. Glucose levels in the whole homogenates were determined with
the glucose GOD-POD (ref.1001192). Lactate was estimated by the lactate LOPOD Kit (ref. 1001330). Triglycerides and total proteins in the whole
homogenates were determined using the triglycerides GPO-POD kit (ref.
100134) and total protein Biuret Kit (ref. 1001291), respectively. Metabolites
ﬁnal concentrations were expressed as mg/g wet weight.
 Enzymes: Aspartate aminotransferase (AAT), alanin aminotransferase activity
(AlAT), alkaline phosphatase (AP) and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) activities
were selected as biomarkers of intermediary metabolism; g-glutamil transpeptidase (g-GT) activity was used as biomarker of induction of oxidative stress
detoxiﬁcation.
AlAT (EC 2.6.1.2.) and AAT (EC 2.6.1.1) were assayed using the kits AlAT (NADH.
Kinetic UV. ref. 1001172) and AAT (NADH. Kinetic UV. ref. 1001172), respectively.
The rate of NADH depletion was determined photometrically (340 nm) as the
catalytic rate concentration of AlAT or AAT, respectively, in the analyzed
sample. The kit AP (p-Nitrophenilphosphate. Kinetic UV. ref. 1001132) was used
to measure AP (EC 3.1.3.1.). The rate of p-nitrophenol formation measured
photometrically (405 nm) is proportional to the catalytic concentration of AP
present in the sample. LDH (EC 1.1.1.27) was assayed with the commercial kit
LDH (Piruvate. Kinetic UV Ref. 1001260). The decrease in concentration of
NADPH as substrate is proportional to the catalytic LDH present in the sample.
g-GT (EC 2.3.2.2.) was analyzed using the commercial kit g-GT (carboxy
substrate. Kinetic. ref. 1001187). The rate of the substrate L-g-glutamyl-3carboxi-4-nitroanilide cleavage to form 5-amine-nitrobenzoic acid was monitored at 405 nm. Enzyme activities were expressed as speciﬁc activities (mmol/
min/mg protein) in crude homogenate.
 Corpulence factor (k): Each ﬁsh was individually weighted wet and measured at
its sampling time. The formula: mass (g)  100/ l3 (cm) was used to calculate
the corpulence factor (De la Torre et al., 2005).

microtiter plate reader (Victor2V 1420-040, Perkin Elmer) was directly
proportional to the amount of Vtg in the sample, four replicates were done.
Final Vtg concentration in the whole samples was expressed as vitellogenin per
protein (ng/mg).
2.8. Statistical analysis
Probit Regression Analysis was used to calculate the 24, 48, 72 and 96 h-LC50
values and its conﬁdence limits (95%). For subacute toxicity test, individual
zebraﬁsh from each tebuconazole experiment were grouped according to exposure
and recovery times. Mean values and standard deviations were calculated for each
test group based on the values obtained for each individual from six ﬁsh. Variables
(no transformed data) were tested for normality (Kolmogorov–Smirnov test with
Lilliefors signiﬁcance correction) and variance homogeneity (Levene’s test). These
results were compared to determine treatment toxic effects by one-way analysis of
variance (ANOVA) and Bonferroni and Duncan’s signiﬁcant difference tests were
used to ﬁnd differences between experimental and control groups. Logarithm
transformation was applied to the variables that failed the Levene test. Tukey’s
honestly signiﬁcant difference (HSD) test was used to assess differences between
the different control groups. In order to see a possible correlation between the
different studied parameters and the time of exposure (experiments 1 and 2),
Pearson’s correlation was used. Statistical analysis was performed using the
Statistical Analysis System (SPSS 15.0) for windows (SPSS, Chicago, IL, USA). The
signiﬁcance level was set at 0.05.

3. Results
3.1. Acute toxicity
Percentages of ﬁsh mortality were calculated for each
fungicide concentration from 24 to 96 h. Based on these results,
median lethal concentration (LC50) values from 24 to 96 h and its
conﬁdence limits were calculated as 23.0 mg/L (20.15–25.60 mg/L)
at 24 h and 19.63 mg/L (18.41–20.80 mg/L) at 48–96 h, respectively.
3.2. Subacute toxicity
Constant sublethal exposure of zebraﬁsh to 230 mg/L of
tebuconazole resulted in disturbance of ﬁsh physiology
(Figs. 1–4). Clear signs of poisoning were observed in all
zebraﬁsh exposed to the fungicide after the ﬁrst hours of
contact with the toxicant, most of these symptoms persisted
during the recovery period. The ﬁsh presented pale color and
reduction in swimming performance followed by long periods of

Experiment 1. The metabolites of intermediary metabolism
measured in the zebraﬁsh after 7 days of exposure to tebuconazole (Fig. 1) showed increases of 135% for glucose from 0.768 mg/g
in control to 1.80 mg/g after exposure, 183% for cholesterol
(control value= 0.42 mg/g; 7 days’ exposure value= 1.19 mg/g)
and 106% for triglycerides (from 2.39 to 4.93 mg/g). Seven days’
lactate levels (1.71 mg/g) also increased by 77% with respect to the
control value (0.97 mg/g). After 7 days of permanency in
pesticide-free water these four metabolites still continued to be
signiﬁcantly increased compared to control values; therefore no
recovery was found during this period. For cholesterol there was
even an increase after 7 days of recovery compared to the value
after 7 days of exposure. Whole-body total proteins remained
stable during the entire experiment. Corpulence factor (k) did not

over the entire experimental set (Fig. 1).
Most enzymatic biomarkers selected as criteria of tebuconazole effect in ﬁsh physiology showed disturbances during the
entire experiment (Fig. 2). Whole-body AAT increased from
2.69 mmol/min/mg protein (controls) to 7.65 mmol/min/mg
protein (+187% increase) in zebraﬁsh after the exposure to
tebuconazole but was re-established after 7 days of recovery period.
AlAT activity (control value =2.39 mmol/min/mg protein) was
strongly increased after the stipulated exposure time. Seven days
in tebuconazole-free water was not enough to allow ﬁsh to
recover normal values. An increase of 197% in AP activity was
registered on the 7th day of exposure to tebuconazole with
respect to the control value (12.75 mmol/min/mg protein). AP
activity remained increased at the end of the recovery period.
LDH levels (control value =50.40 mmol/min/mg protein)
showed disturbances that were statistically signiﬁcant after 7
days of exposure but was recovered after 7 days of recovery period
(Fig. 2).
g-GT activity slightly increased on the 7th day of exposure but
did not show any signiﬁcant difference between exposed zebraﬁsh
and control animals (0.28 mmol/min/mg protein) as response of
the presence of tebuconazole in the water (Fig. 2). Therefore,
during the recovery period differences between pre-exposed and
control ﬁsh were statistically not signiﬁcant.
Experiment 2. Fourteen days of tebuconazole exposure induced
in zebraﬁsh the highest increases in both glucose (158%) and
cholesterol (130%) levels (Fig. 3). Increases over 60% vs. controls
(2.39 mg/g) were determined for triglycerides (4.96 mg/g), and
lactate levels were increased by 80% (1.51 mg/g) with respect to
the control values (0.97 mg/g). Values for glucose and cholesterol
were still signiﬁcantly increased after 7 days of recovery but were
re-established after 14 days of recovery while triglycerides and
lactate remained high after this time in clean water. Whole-body
total proteins measured in zebraﬁsh remained stable along the
entire experimental time. Corpulence factor (k) did not shown any
signiﬁcant difference with control during the entire experiment,
as in experiment 1.
Several enzymatic biomarkers (Fig. 4) changed as a consequence of tebuconazole ﬁsh intoxication.

4. Discussion
Acute toxicity of tebuconazole on the zebraﬁsh D. rerio in the
present study resulted in LC50 values ranging from 23.0 mg/L
(24 h) to 19.7 mg/L (48–96 h).
If we compare these results with those found in the literature
with the same fungicide in other ﬁsh species, we found out D. rerio
is less sensitive to tebuconazole than O. mykiss (4.4 mg/L) or
Lepomis macrochirus (5.7 mg/L) (Tomlin, 2000). According to the
LC50 values obtained in our laboratory, tebuconazole is also less
toxic to D. rerio than other fungicides as tricyclazole (Sancho et al.,
2009a) or prochloraz (unpublished data) in the same species.

The following clinical symptoms were observed in zebraﬁsh
exposed to tebuconazole: loss of movement coordination, dullness, ﬁsh lay-down at their ﬂank, resting stage at the tank bottom
and pale color. These symptoms are currently cited in other ﬁsh
species during the toxic stress induced by other pesticides (Karan
et al., 1998; Peña et al., 2000; Sancho et al, 2009b). However, when
other authors such as Konwick et al (2006) exposed rainbow trout
for 8 days to tebuconazole, no sign of toxic stress was found.
Although ﬁsh used in the subacute toxicity present study were
fed, the uptake of tebuconazole from the water took place
principally through gills due its high water solubility (Andreu
et al., under review). Gills uptake plays an important role in the
incorporation of pesticides via blood to other organs like liver.
As a consequence of tebuconazole exposure, intermediary
metabolism of zebraﬁsh was altered as a physiological strategy
played by ﬁsh against the toxicant. Glucose increases directly
correlate with enhanced levels of glycemia required in ﬁsh
submitted to stress condition (Heath, 1995). This leads to the
stimulation of processes as lipolysis or proteolysis to use the
degraded products as disposable for energy. An interesting feature
in tebuconazole-treated zebraﬁsh was the release of triglycerides
that were increased during the entire experimental period.
Contrarily, Konwick et al. (2006) exposed rainbow trout to
tebuconazole-contaminated food and did not ﬁnd signiﬁcant
differences in lipid percentage or liver somatic index between
treatment and control ﬁsh on any sampling day. These authors
also referred that there were no signs of stress or mortality in
either treatment.
Mobilization of lipids reserves as triglycerides undergone by
the animals testiﬁes high-energy demands. Such increase of
energy demand was conﬁrmed by the increases in whole-body
triglycerides, cholesterol, glucose and lactate, to overcome the
stress. The stimulation of lipid catabolism includes the formation
of lipoproteins that are utilized to repair cell-damaged and tissue
organelles, direct utilization by cells for energy requirements and
increased lypolyses. Finally, this depletion of energy reserves may
have its consequences for higher levels of biological organization,
like diminished growth, survival probability and reproduction
(Roex et al., 2003). In mammals, lipid metabolism as cholesterol
biosynthesis pathway has been referred as disrupted by triazoles
(Hester and Nesnow, 2008). It has been demonstrated in carp
(Cyprinus carpio) that exposure to phenol (an endocrine disruptor)
caused signiﬁcant increase of non-steriﬁed cholesterol due to the
inability of the steroidogenic tissues to synthesize steroids
(Mukherjee et al., 1991).
Increases of LDH activity were found during both experiments.
Enhancement of anaerobic metabolism is a rapid and clear
response against depletion of energy caused by lack of oxygen.
LDH forms the center of a delicately balanced equilibrium
between catabolism and anabolism of carbohydrates. Raised
LDH activity is a marker for tissue damage in ﬁsh and serves as
a good diagnostic tool in Toxicology (Rao, 2006). Our results show
that fungicide effect on ﬁsh LDH activity was maintained even
after 14 days of recovery in fungicide-free water. Lactate is the end
product of glycolysis under hypoxic conditions. The high levels of
lactate measured during our experiments indicate metabolic
disorders, which persisted even during the recovery periods.
Similar results were found in zebraﬁsh exposed to the fungicide
tricyclazole (Sancho et al., 2009a). However, other toxicants such
as prochloraz seem to exert a strong inhibition on LDH activity of
the same ﬁsh (Sancho et al., unpublished data). Borges et al.
(2007) showed that the LDH activity in the ﬁsh Rhamdia quelen
did not change or showed a non-signiﬁcant increase when
exposed to the pesticide cypermethrin. However, propanil
exposure of the ﬁsh Anguilla anguilla resulted in an increase of
the lactate levels as determined by Sancho et al. (2009b).

Tebuconazole signiﬁcantly increased the activities AAT and
AlAT in zebraﬁsh. The levels of AlAT rapidly recover when animals
were transferred to clean water. ALT is a speciﬁc enzyme to test
liver hepatocytes (Ramaia, 2007). Disturbances on functional
enzymes as AAT, AlAT and AP allow the identiﬁcation of tissue
damage in organs such as liver (Karan et al., 1998; Begum, 2004;
De la Torre et al., 2005; Borges et al., 2007). Some authors such as
De la Torre et al. (2005) determined that an increase in hepatic
transaminases AlAT and AAT levels in the ﬁsh Cnesterodon
decemmaculatus could be used as biomarkers of exposure to
pesticide-polluted waters.
Tebuconazole increased AP activity in the zebraﬁsh as is shown
in the present study. The results agree with those found by Borges
et al. (2007) when R. quelen wad exposed to cypermethrin. Similar
results were obtained by Rao (2006) in tilapia (Oreochromis
mossambicus) as a consequence of exposure to the insecticide
2-butenoicacid-3-(diethoxyphosphinothioyl) methyl ester (RPR-II);
they also found a recovery of AP activity after 7 days of depuration
period. However, in the present study, AAT and AP continued to
increase at the end of the experiments.
Total proteins content measured in the whole-body homogenates did not show any signiﬁcant difference from controls
neither corpulence factor (k), which was also unaltered over the
entire experiments. Our results are in agreement with those found
by Roex et al. (2003): when D. rerio was exposed to parathion for
250 days, the authors reported ﬁsh stress, but whole-body
proteins did not decrease. k is a morphological parameter that is
indicative of the health status of the ﬁsh and normally is related to
the environmental availability of food. As a parameter to assess
the general condition of the ﬁsh, our results did not show
signiﬁcant alterations, regardless of the time and the fungicide
concentration tested. Our results agree with those obtained by
Kinnberg et al. (2007) when D. rerio was exposed to the fungicide
prochloraz. However, ﬁsh exposure to the triazole tricyclazole
(Sancho et al., 2009a) showed an effect on the corpulence factor k,
which indicated an effect on somatic growth. Corpulence factor is
a physiological index of the ﬁsh health status related to the
environmental availability of food, but it may be possible that it
could be affected by other factors related to the presence of toxic
substances in the media (De la Torre et al., 2005).
An enhancement of the g-GT levels in zebraﬁsh whole-body
was only observed during the recovery period of experiment 2.
This enhancement of g-GT could indicate an adaptative response
to oxidative stress and suggest an activation of the release of g-GT

375

from liver to other tissues. Sancho et al (2009b) found an
activation of the release of g-GT from liver to other tissues, which
was correlated by an increase in muscle g-GT vs. a decrease of
liver g-GT when A. anguilla was exposed to sublethal concentrations of the herbicide propanil. As g-GT is implied in the
glutathione metabolism, our results could indicate that compensatory protective mechanisms that provide defense against lipid
damage/or repair damaged lipids had been activated as prooxidant/antioxidant balance of the glutathione redox cycle. Peña
et al. (2000) and Favari et al. (2002) related the increases in g-GT
activities as a detoxiﬁcation process response in A. anguilla and
Chirostoma riojai exposed to pesticides, respectively.
Scarce data are disposable about the possible endocrine
disruptive effects of tebuconazole in ﬁsh. The fungicidal effect of
triazoles as well as the structurally related imidazole fungicides is
a result of the inhibition of cytochrome P450 (Kinnberg et al.,
2007). Thyroid tissues and hormones in mammals are also
affected by triazoles (Taxvig et al., 2007, 2008, Hester and
Nesnow, 2008). The disturbance of the key enzymes like CYP17
involved in the synthesis of steroid hormones has been indicated
as a mechanism for the endocrine-disrupting effect of tebuconazole among other azole fungicides (Taxvig et al., 2007, 2008).
We found an increase in vitellogenesis as a consequence of
tebuconazole exposure in zebraﬁsh males from both the experiments (1 and 2). Our results agree with those found by Kinnberg
et al (2007), which demonstrated the estrogenic effects of
prochloraz by inducing vitellogenesis in D. rerio males exposed
to different fungicide concentrations. Tricyclazole also induced
vitellogenesis in male zebraﬁsh under subacute exposure in the
laboratory (Sancho et al., 2009a). The direct consequences of
vitellogenin synthesis in males are poorly understood, but it can
be mentioned that there is a reduction in scales and skeleton
calcium, liver hyperplasia/hypertrophy and kidney damage (Herman and Kincaid, 1988). Secondary sexual characteristics and
body markings may also not develop properly, leading to
abnormal or absent reproductive behavior (Jones and Reynolds,
1997).
Endocrine disrupting chemicals affect sexual development and
reproduction in wildlife, via several pathways. The sex hormone
balance depends on the availability and activity of the steroid
synthesizing enzymes, and in particular on the CYP19 aromatase,
which catalyzes the conversion of androgens to estrogens
(Kinnberg et al., 2007). It is obvious that the short-term
reproductive impacts of xenoestrogen exposure in juvenile or
adult male ﬁsh, outside the breeding season, could induce the
inappropriate synthesis of vitellogenin (Arukwe, 2001).
Taxvig et al. (2007) demonstrated the anti-androgenic effect of
tebuconazole when the feminization of male offspring rats was
induced as a consequence of the exposure of the mother to
tebuconazole. Tebuconazole has also been cited as a potential
neurotoxicant (Filipov and Lawrence, 2001) that might result in
functional endocrine and immune alterations, which necessitates
further studies that address toxicant effects on interorgan-system
communication.

5. Conclusion
The present results suggested that lipid and carbohydrate
metabolism as well as several enzymatic activities are affected in
zebraﬁsh as a consequence of the exposure to the fungicide
tebuconazole. The selected biomarkers were useful to demonstrate
impaired endocrine networks together with the effect of this
toxicant on ﬁsh vitellogenin production. Further research may be
necessary to adequately assess the physiological state of the ﬁsh
under tebuconazole stress. We call for exhaustible and mechanistic
